Neonatal dugongs, referred to as calves, are born after a gestation period of 374 days [tg = 374 days] under typical tropical water temperatures of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C]. At the moment of parturition, a newborn calf measures approximately 110 cm [Lb = approximately 110 cm] in total length and has a wet birth weight of about 27,500 grams [Wwb = about 27,500 grams]. This substantial initial size, characteristic of a precocial neonate, allows the calf to swim alongside its mother almost immediately after delivery. The relatively long gestation, when compared to other sirenians, is thought to facilitate the development of a large, robust offspring capable of navigating shallow seagrass meadows. Field observations from the waters around Australia and the Indo-Pacific indicate that the strong mother-calf bond is established within hours of the birth event, with the calf beginning to nurse shortly thereafter. The nursing offspring remains in close association with the adult female, relying entirely on her milk for the first several months of life. This initial investment in a single, large calf represents a key life-history strategy for a species that inhabits a nutrient-poor, yet stable, environment.

The suckling juvenile phase in Dugong dugon is marked by a prolonged period of maternal dependence that extends well beyond the first year of life. Detailed records from field studies in Moreton Bay, Australia, suggest that the time since birth at weaning is approximately 548 days [tx = approximately 548 days], occurring at a water temperature of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C]. This extended nursing stage, during which the calf gradually transitions to a diet of seagrasses, is critical for learning foraging techniques and developing the gut flora necessary to digest fibrous plant material. Older calves have been observed swimming with their mothers while the adult female uproots rhizomes, thereby facilitating the nutritional independence onset of the young. The eventual cessation of milk ingestion marks a major dietary transition for the juvenile, after which it must rely entirely on its own foraging abilities. Weaned individuals begin to explore seagrass beds more independently, though they may still remain within the general home range of the mother for a period. This prolonged weaning period is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in other large marine herbivores such as the manatee.

Sexual maturation in the dugong occurs relatively late, with puberty being reached at a total length that differs between the sexes. For females, the total length at puberty is 239 cm [Lp = 239 cm], whereas males achieve this developmental milestone at a slightly larger size of 240 cm [Lp = 240 cm]. This measurement suggests that females begin to mature at a marginally smaller body size than their male counterparts, a pattern that is not uncommon among large mammals. The time since birth at puberty is reported to be approximately 3,470 days [tp = approximately 3,470 days], as estimated from growth curves and capture-mark-recapture data collected under ambient tropical conditions of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C]. This extended period to reach reproductive maturity — nearly a decade — underscores the species' remarkably slow pace of life. Before reaching this stage, the sub-adult individual undergoes a prolonged period of somatic growth, during which it must accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of future gestation and lactation. The onset of gonad maturation likely coincides with the achievement of this critical body length, signaling readiness for reproductive activity.

Adult body size in Dugong dugon exhibits a notable sexual dimorphism, with females attaining larger ultimate dimensions than males. The ultimate total length for females reaches up to 305 cm [Li = up to 305 cm], while males achieve a slightly smaller maximum of 270 cm [Li = 270 cm]. Consistent with this length disparity, the ultimate wet weight for females is 519,000 grams [Wwi = 519,000 grams], substantially heavier than the 360,000 grams [Wwi = 360,000 grams] recorded for males. This pronounced size difference is a hallmark of a mating system where larger females may be favored for their capacity to gestate and nurse a large calf, despite the high energetic costs associated with such a slow-growing lifestyle. The massive body mass of an adult female, reaching over half a metric ton, allows for significant fat storage, which is crucial during periods of food scarcity in the seagrass ecosystem. In terms of reproductive output, females typically produce a single calf per litter [N_R_i = single calf per litter], with a low annual frequency of approximately 0.2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.2 litters per year]. This translates to a maximum reproductive rate of 0.2 calves per year [Ri = 0.2 calves per year], reflecting an extremely slow fecundity schedule.

The overall lifespan of the dugong is remarkably long for a marine mammal of its size, with a maximum recorded longevity of approximately 73 years [am = approximately 73 years] under typical tropical conditions of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C]. This extended lifespan is a critical component of its slow life-history strategy, compensating for the very low annual reproductive output by allowing individuals to breed over many decades. The combination of a 374-day gestation period (374 days) [tg = 374 days], a weaning age of 548 days after birth [tx = 548 days after birth], and a delayed puberty at around 3,470 days after birth [tp = around 3,470 days after birth], all occurring at a stable temperature of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C], results in one of the longest intergenerational intervals among all marine mammals. This suite of life-history traits renders the species exceptionally vulnerable to anthropogenic threats such as boat strikes, habitat degradation, and incidental capture in fishing gear, because population recovery from any decline is extremely slow. Given that a female produces less than one calf every five years, even modest increases in adult mortality can lead to rapid population declines. Conservation efforts for this species must therefore prioritize the protection of adult females and their critical seagrass foraging habitats to ensure long-term population viability.
